1.q: What is Python, and why is it so popular?
1.a: A high-level, general-purpose language (Guido van Rossum, 1991) built to be easy to read. Popular because the code is short and readable, there is a library for almost everything (NumPy, pandas, PyTorch, FastAPI), it runs on every OS, and you can write procedural, object-oriented or functional code. Used for AI/ML, data, web backends and automation.
1.hook: Write the idea, not the ceremony.

1.q: Is Python compiled or interpreted?
1.a: Both. CPython first compiles your code to bytecode, then the Python Virtual Machine (PVM) interprets that bytecode. It is called interpreted because you never run a separate compile step and you never get an .exe.
1.hook: Compiled into step cards, then a cook follows the cards.

1.q: What happens when you run `python app.py`?
1.a: 1. Python checks the grammar of the whole file; a SyntaxError stops everything before line 1 runs. 2. It compiles the code to bytecode (saved as .pyc in __pycache__ for imported modules). 3. The PVM carries out the bytecode one instruction at a time; NameError, TypeError and other runtime errors happen here. The PVM does not turn bytecode into machine code; only a JIT does that.
1.hook: Grammar is checked before cooking; missing ingredients are found while cooking.

1.q: What is a dynamically typed language? Is Python strongly typed too?
1.a: Dynamic: types are checked while the program runs, and a variable can point to any type, so `x = 5` then `x = "five"` is fine. Strong: Python never silently mixes unrelated types, so `"1" + 1` is a TypeError (JavaScript would give "11"). Python is both dynamic and strong.
1.out:
<class 'str'>
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
1.hook: Labels can move (dynamic); apples and oranges never mix (strong).

1.q: How do variables work in Python?
1.a: A variable is a label stuck on an object, not a box that holds a value. Every value is an object with a type and an identity (`type(x)`, `id(x)`). Two labels can point to the same object, so a change made through one shows up through the other.
1.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a, a is b)

1.q: How is memory managed in Python?
1.a: Automatically. Each object counts the labels (references) pointing to it, and when the count reaches zero it is freed straight away. A garbage collector also cleans up groups of objects that only point at each other (reference cycles). All objects live in Python's private heap, which CPython manages for you.
1.hook: Count the labels; zero labels means thrown away.

1.q: What is the GIL?
1.a: The Global Interpreter Lock: in standard CPython only one thread runs Python code at a time. Threads still help with waiting work (downloads, API calls) but not with heavy CPU work; use multiprocessing for that. Since 3.14 there is an official free-threaded build without the GIL.
1.hook: One knife in the kitchen: many cooks, one cutting at a time.

1.q: Why is Python slower than C, and why is it still used for AI?
1.a: Slower because it checks types on every operation while running, and the PVM reads instructions one by one; C checks types once, when it compiles. AI still uses Python because Python only directs the work, while the heavy maths runs in C, C++ or CUDA inside NumPy and PyTorch. Measured: adding 10 million numbers took about 0.46 s with a Python loop and 0.007 s with NumPy.
1.hook: Python checks every time; C checks once. Python is the manager, C is the worker.

1.q: What is a docstring? How is it different from a comment?
1.a: A docstring is a string written as the first line inside a function, class or module. Python keeps it in `__doc__` and `help()` shows it, so it tells people how to use the code. A `#` comment is thrown away by Python and explains why the code does something.

1.q: Why is indentation required in Python?
1.a: Python uses indentation instead of `{ }` to mark blocks: everything indented under a line ending in `:` belongs to it. Wrong indentation is an error, not a style problem: IndentationError, or TabError if tabs and spaces are mixed. Use 4 spaces.

1.q: Line 2 is indented with a Tab, line 3 with 8 spaces. Which error?
1.out: TabError: inconsistent use of tabs and spaces in indentation
1.why: They look the same on screen, but Python refuses to guess how wide a Tab is. Use 4 spaces everywhere.

1.q: Which is a valid variable name?
1.why: Names use letters, digits and `_`, can't start with a digit, can't contain `-`, and can't be a keyword.

1.q: Which of these is NOT a Python keyword?
1.why: `print` is a built-in function, not a keyword. Python has 35 keywords, and `True`, `False` and `None` are among them.

1.q: When does Python save `.pyc` files in `__pycache__`?
options: Every time you run any .py file
Only for the script you run directly
Never: Python 3 has no bytecode files
1.why: The script you run directly is compiled in memory only. Imported modules get their bytecode saved so the next import is faster.

1.q: What does the PVM do with bytecode?
options: Converts it into machine code and saves an .exe
Carries out each instruction itself, one by one
Sends it to a C compiler
Turns it back into Python source
1.why: The PVM is a C program that reads and performs each bytecode instruction. Only a JIT turns bytecode into machine code.

1.q: Which is true about Python's typing?
1.why: Types are checked while running (dynamic), and unrelated types are never mixed silently (strong).

1.q: What's the right way to check if `x` is None?
1.why: There is only one None object, so check identity with `is`. A class can change what `==` means and give a wrong answer.
